title: Alpine launches bid to overturn Pierre Gasly’s Monaco F1 penalties
content:
MONACO — Alpine has moved to overturn Pierre Gasly’s time penalties that cost him a podium finish in Sunday’s Monaco Grand Prix by lodging a right of review with Formula 1 race stewards.

Gasly crossed the line third for Alpine, but was demoted to seventh place after receiving two five-second time penalties for breaking the pit lane speed limit.

The 30-year-old was one of five drivers to receive a penalty during Sunday’s race for pit lane speeding, where the limit is set at 60 km/h (37.2 mph). Gasly exceeded the limit by 0.1 km/h and 0.4 km/h in his two sanctions.

Speaking to reporters after the race, Gasly suggested that Alpine may look to challenge the stewards’ ruling, saying: “Hopefully they can do something.” At the time, he was unsure whether the team had commenced that process.

But in a short statement issued one hour later, an Alpine spokesperson said the team had lodged a right of review with the FIA-appointed stewards in Monaco.

Through this process, Alpine will be required to bring new and significant evidence before the stewards. If the evidence is deemed to meet those conditions, they will be able to re-evaluate the penalties which, if overturned, would restore Gasly to third place.

“I don’t think there’s anything that would hurt me more right now,” Gasly had told reporters after the race.

“It’s 10 years I’m f—ing working my ass off for this type of moment. We did everything right today. Standing on that podium in front of all the fans that turn up, this is the type of moment that for me can’t be taken away from us by unfair reasons.

“What’s going on right now is not right and hopefully they can make the right calls.”

There were eight in-race penalties on Sunday in Monaco, six of which were for pit lane speeding.

On top of Gasly’s pair of speeding penalties, Lewis Hamilton received the same sanction — which he served during the race and still finished second — while Oscar Piastri, Franco Colapinto and George Russell also received the same penalty.

“I was shocked to hear that I was speeding because I wasn’t actually above the speed,” Hamilton said, with the stewards saying he was 0.1 km/h above the limit. Russell, Colapinto and Piastri’s offences were also just 0.1 km/h over the 60 km/h limit.

“I think it’s the (average) distance,” said Hamilton. “(It’s) something that we really need to look into, because I heard lots of people got that today and they probably weren’t really speeding.”

Pit lane speeding is rare in F1 races. Drivers will try to come down to the limit as late as possible when entering the pits, where a white line marks the point at which their speed is assessed.

The speed is taken as an average in the ‘fast lane’ from pit entry to pit exit. It effectively works like an average speed zone on a highway. Drivers will use a pit lane speed limiter button on their steering wheel when they cross the white line to enter the pit lane.

The Monaco pit entry requires drivers to turn right as they cross the white line, before then steering left to turn toward the garages. As they do so, drivers will typically cut across the white line that keeps the ‘fast lane’ to the right-hand side to make it easier to negotiate the entry before proceeding to their garages.

But in cutting the white line on the left-hand side, it effectively shortens the distance of the pit lane — which would mean the speed must be slightly lower as a result.

The same is true at pit exit, too. Drivers are able to cut the white line as they steer left past the Cadillac garage before leaving the pit lane and returning to the track.

The tactic has been common in Monaco for years, making the slew of penalties a surprise for the drivers.

“I think it’s just the way the pit lane is,” said Hamilton. “I’ve done this pit lane for years. It’s not like I came in and didn’t press the button or something like that. (The) pit lane limiter is on immediately.

“It’s just the line that you take, which is the same line we’ve all taken for years where you come in. You kind of cut part of the white line.”

Piastri said he went “as wide as I could through the whole pit lane, and I still got done.” The Australian finished the race fourth for McLaren, having moved above Gasly after the Alpine driver was penalized.

“I got told that a lot of people had been done for speeding,” said Piastri. “I was still basically exiting Rascasse when I hit the pit speed limiter. And then yeah, obviously if you take a shorter distance, that can trigger it sometimes.

“But I was very safe with all of that. A very strange one.”

Russell referred to a “software glitch” when discussing his speeding sanction. Mercedes’ failure to correctly serve the penalty when Russell pitted led to a drive-through penalty which, after the red flag restart, dropped him outside of the points.

“I probably, with the software glitch, gained one-tenth of a second in the whole pit lane and lost 13 positions,” said Russell.
